q1.question: What does a website cost?
q1.answer: A professional landing page starts at $850, a five-to-eight section corporate site from $1,200, and an online store from $1,750. What moves the price is integrations, not page count. You get a fixed scope and a written price after the first call, before any work begins. Figures shown are for reference only.

q2.question: How long does it take?
q2.answer: Three to six weeks for a landing page or corporate site, five to eight for a store with a catalog. What usually stretches a timeline is not development but waiting on copy, photos and access, so at kickoff we tell you exactly what we need from you and when.

q3.question: Who owns the site and the code?
q3.answer: You do, from day one. Domain, hosting, repository, analytics and ad accounts are registered in your name with us granted access. There is nothing to reclaim if the relationship ends, and no part of the build is held as leverage. It is also better practice for your historical data.

q4.question: Can we manage it ourselves afterwards?
q4.answer: Yes. The site ships with an admin panel for text, images and posts, plus a recorded handover session. Ongoing maintenance is available as a separate service, but it is an option rather than a condition — you are not required to keep paying us to keep the site running.

q5.question: Is domain and hosting included?
q5.answer: For the first year: domain, SSL certificate and professional hosting are in the package. From year two hosting is billed separately, roughly $10 to $35 per month depending on traffic and platform, or you can move it to your own provider with no penalty. Figures shown are for reference only.

q6.question: Does it include SEO?
q6.answer: The technical foundation does: speed, clean URL structure, metadata, structured data and analytics wired up at launch. Ongoing SEO — monthly content, links, tracking — is a separate service, because it is continuous work rather than a deliverable. Building the foundation in from the start is far cheaper than retrofitting it.

q7.question: We already have a site. Rebuild or fix?
q7.answer: We look before recommending. Often a rebuild is not needed: fixing speed, correcting structure and adding what is missing costs considerably less and keeps the authority the domain already earned. A rebuild is justified when the current site is slow, fails on mobile or cannot be measured — problems no amount of content will offset.

q8.question: How does payment work?
q8.answer: In U.S. dollars, usually half at kickoff and half at launch, by transfer or card, invoiced through our U.S. subsidiary. Scope, dates and revision rounds are written down before we start, so nothing changes shape halfway through.

q9.question: What if we need changes later?
q9.answer: Every project includes two revision rounds before launch and thirty days of warranty on anything that breaks afterwards. Changes that come up later are quoted separately or covered by a maintenance plan, depending on how much work they involve.

q10.question: Do you handle U.S. payments and sales tax?
q10.answer: Yes. We configure the gateway you use — Stripe, PayPal or the platform's own — and set up state-level tax calculation, which is the piece most commonly left broken. Filing returns remains yours; what we make sure of is that collection is correct from the first order.

q1.question: What does a digital marketing agency like 3R Core actually do?
q1.answer: We design websites, manage your social media, run Google Ads campaigns, position your brand on Google through SEO and develop your visual identity (branding). We work as your external marketing team: strategy + execution + monthly data-driven reports.

q2.question: Do you work with U.S. clients remotely?
q2.answer: Yes. Our in-house team works U.S. business hours, and U.S. clients contract through our U.S. subsidiary. Everything runs remotely with video meetings and online reports: 60% of our projects are 100% remote.

q3.question: How much does it cost to hire a digital marketing agency?
q3.answer: It depends on the service and scope. As reference for US clients: our SEO plan starts at $500/month; Google Ads campaigns from $800/month + ad spend; social media management from $800/month; websites from $850. In our first meeting we deliver a tailored quote.

q4.question: How long does it take to see real results?
q4.answer: It depends on the service. SEO consolidates within three to six months of consistent work. A website starts producing from the day it launches, provided measurement was installed before launch and not after. An online store depends on how you bring traffic to it. In the United States 3R Core sells three services — websites, SEO and online stores — and we give you clear KPIs from day one for each of them.

q5.question: Why choose 3R Core over another agency?
q5.answer: We are a 3-generation family agency (3R = the three Roque brothers) combining traditional experience with technology and digital-native vision. Every client works directly with a director, not a junior account. Transparent monthly reports and no forced long-term contracts.

q6.question: Do I need to have my brand ready or can you help me build it?
q6.answer: Both. If you already have branding, we respect it and build on top. If you start from scratch, our Branding team creates your logo, visual identity, brand book and every piece needed for your business to compete strongly online.

q7.question: How do I choose the best digital marketing agency for my business?
q7.answer: Five filters that actually matter: 1) verifiable portfolio of projects similar to yours, 2) monthly reports with real metrics (not vanity metrics), 3) signed NDA and account ownership (your Google Ads, GA4 and social accounts stay yours), 4) a director joins the conversation, not just a junior account manager, and 5) real Google reviews and published case studies. At 3R Core we tick all 5.

q8.question: Should I hire an agency or several freelancers?
q8.answer: For small, very specific projects a freelancer can work. For a full strategy (brand + web + social + ads + SEO) an agency gives you coordination, a multidisciplinary team, continuity if someone leaves and a real process. Quick math: hiring 4 freelancers (designer, dev, community, ads specialist) usually costs the same or more than an agency, with zero coordination between them.

q9.question: How much should I invest monthly in digital marketing?
q9.answer: As a 2026 reference: startups $750–1,400/month (covers social + basic ads), SMBs $1,500–3,600 (integrated strategy with social, ads, SEO and web improvements), mid-size companies $3,600–9,000 (full marketing with content production and CRO). What matters is not the budget itself but that ROI is positive by month 3.

q10.question: What happens to my Google Ads, Meta Ads and Analytics accounts if I leave the agency?
q10.answer: They are 100% yours, always. At 3R Core we create accounts under your name and we manage them with management permissions. If you decide to switch agencies or move in-house, you keep the entire history, creatives, saved audiences and full configuration. Zero locks.

q2.question: How long does a complete branding project take?
q2.answer: We deliver a full branding project in 7 business days, with a clear milestone timeline: discovery, proposals, refinement and final delivery with all editable files. If the scope grows (corporate rebranding, extensive manuals, special applications) we agree on a longer timeline before kickoff.

q3.question: How much does designing my brand identity cost?
q3.answer: Branding projects at 3R Core start at $500 USD for US clients and scale according to corporate scope. We deliver a formal quote with detailed deliverables after an initial discovery session. Figures shown are for reference only.

q4.question: If I only want a logo, can you do that?
q4.answer: Yes, we offer individual logo packages. However, we always recommend full branding: an isolated logo, without a visual system or manual, tends to lose strength and ends up being applied poorly across social media, web and ads.

q5.question: Will I receive the editable logo and brand manual files?
q5.answer: Yes, with no locks or restrictions. You receive vector files (.AI, .EPS, .SVG), .PDF for print, .PNG/.JPG for web, and the complete brand manual. The identity is 100% yours after delivery.

q6.question: Do you work with companies that already have a brand but want to redesign it?
q6.answer: Yes, we do rebranding and brand refresh. We audit the current identity, preserve valuable assets and modernize what no longer works. It's a more careful intervention because we must protect existing brand recognition.

q7.question: How do I choose a branding agency?
q7.answer: Always ask for 3 things before signing: 1) portfolio of projects in industries similar to yours, 2) written deliverables list (how many files, what formats, brand book length), and 3) timeline with clear milestones. A serious agency proposes a discovery session BEFORE quoting; a sloppy one throws a price without asking anything about your business.

q8.question: What's the difference between logo design, visual identity and branding?
q8.answer: Logo is just the icon/symbol. Visual identity is the full system (logo + colors + typography + iconography). Branding is the brand strategy (positioning, value proposition, tone of voice, architecture) plus that visual identity applied at every touchpoint. Asking for 'just a logo' is usually false economy: it ends up costing more when the entire visual system needs to be redone.

q9.question: What if I don't like any of the logo proposals?
q9.answer: We work with 2 included revision rounds: in the first we present 3 distinct concepts in black and white; we refine the chosen one in color and applications. If after the first round no concept convinces, we adjust the brief and iterate again at no additional cost. It's very rare: prior discovery gives us 80% of the work well-oriented.

q10.question: Does my brand need rebranding or just a refresh?
q10.answer: Refresh: if your logo looks dated but the brand is still recognized (modernize typography, simplify, adjust colors). Rebranding: if your value proposition changed, if the target audience is different, if you merged with another company, or if the brand has negative associations. We do a free initial audit and tell you which one applies.

intro.title: Why UGC beats polished production on cost per result
intro.p1: UGC is advertising shot to look like organic content: vertical, natural light, a real person talking to camera. It doesn't replace your brand film. It replaces the ad people scroll past.
intro.p2: The advantage is economic, not aesthetic. A traditional spot costs thousands and yields one asset. The same budget in UGC yields eight to twenty variations — and on platforms that optimize by creative, volume of variations is precisely what drives cost per result down.
intro.p3: We work with in-house creators, not a marketplace. That means we control the brief, the turnaround and the reshoot. If an angle underperforms, we shoot it again without renegotiating rates with a third party — and you get U.S.-agency output at nearshore cost.

items.title: Angle research
items.description: Before anyone films, we define the selling angles: problem, objection, comparison, demonstration and social proof. Each angle is a testable hypothesis, not a mood board.

items.title: Scripted, hook first

items.title: Creator matched to buyer
items.description: We cast by your customer profile — age, tone, context. The same face shouldn't be selling supplements and B2B software.

items.title: Editing and variations

q2.question: How many videos do I need to start?
q2.answer: A first batch of six to ten assets is the practical minimum. Below that you have nothing to compare: if you test two videos and both underperform, you can't tell whether the format or the angle failed. q1.question: What's the difference between PR and advertising?
q1.answer: In advertising you buy the space and control the message. In PR you earn the space and give up part of that control in exchange for credibility: the reader knows the outlet chose to publish it. That difference is exactly why an editorial mention carries more weight than an ad of the same size, and also why publication can never be guaranteed.

q2.question: Can you guarantee coverage in a specific outlet?
q2.answer: No, and be wary of anyone who does. What's guaranteed is the work: the media map, the angles, the materials, the outreach and the follow-up. The decision to publish belongs to the outlet. When someone guarantees a placement, what they're actually selling is paid space — a legitimate product, but a different one, with far less credibility value.

q3.question: What counts as news inside my company?
q3.answer: More than most people think, but almost never what the company wants to say. Launching a product isn't news. Proprietary data that reveals something about the market is. So is an industry figure nobody has published, a verifiable milestone, a contestable position, or a specific human story. Finding that inside the business is part of the work.

q4.question: Does PR help SEO?
q4.answer: Yes, two ways. First, links: a mention in an authoritative outlet is among the hardest links to earn and among the heaviest in weight. Second, brand: when people start searching your name after reading about you, Google reads those searches as a signal of a recognized entity, which benefits rankings across the whole domain.

q5.question: How long until results?

PR compounds: the second mention costs less effort than the first because the reporter already knows you, and from month three you start receiving inbound requests instead of only sending pitches.

q6.question: What happens during a reputation crisis?
q6.answer: The first rule is not improvising while it's hot. We establish verified facts, decide who speaks and through which channel, draft a position, and respond quickly but once — avoiding feeding the cycle. Most crises worsen not because of the original event but because of contradictory responses issued by several people in the first hours.
